source_evidence.anchor: Remark 2.7.9, title and paragraph beginning 'You may be surprised' through the displayed Taylor approximation
source_evidence.observation: The remark motivates the shared near-origin MGF behavior, assumes for simplicity that X is bounded in addition to having mean zero and unit variance, and displays the approximation E exp(lambda X) approximately E[1 + lambda X + lambda^2 X^2/2 + o(lambda^2 X^2)] = 1 + lambda^2/2 approximately exp(lambda^2/2) as lambda tends to zero.

source_evidence.anchor: Remark 2.7.9 continuation, from 'becomes an equality' through '(Check this!)'
source_evidence.observation: The continuation states that the approximation is equality for N(0,1), contrasts the all-lambda sub-gaussian bound with the small-lambda sub-exponential bound, says that each respective bound characterizes its distribution class, and states that the MGF of X distributed as Exp(1) is infinite for lambda at least one.

Equation (2.12) gives E exp(lambda X) = exp(lambda^2/2) for X distributed as N(0,1) and every real lambda; Proposition 2.5.2(v), under E X = 0, gives the sub-gaussian MGF condition E exp(lambda X) <= exp(K_5^2 lambda^2) for every real lambda.

Under E X = 0, the sub-exponential MGF condition is E exp(lambda X) <= exp(K_5^2 lambda^2) for all lambda satisfying |lambda| <= 1/K_5; it is equivalent, up to absolute-constant changes of parameters, to the other sub-exponential properties in that proposition.

source_evidence.anchor: Example 2.7.8, definition and parameter summary for the exponential distribution
source_evidence.observation: The surrounding source defines X distributed as Exp(lambda) as nonnegative with tail P{X >= t} = exp(-lambda t) for t >= 0, identifies exponential distributions as sub-exponential, and records mean and standard deviation of order 1/lambda.

binders: For the local Taylor claim, X is a random variable and lambda is a real parameter tending to 0 (PDF page 23; printed page 34, Remark 2.7.9 displayed approximation).

For the exact comparison, X has the standard normal distribution N(0,1) and lambda ranges over all real numbers (PDF page 13; printed page 24, equation (2.12); PDF page 24; printed page 35, Remark 2.7.9 continuation).

For the class comparisons, X is respectively a centered sub-gaussian or centered sub-exponential random variable, with a positive MGF scale parameter K_5 (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(v); PDF page 21; printed page 32, Proposition 2.7.1(e)).
For the failure example, X has distribution Exp(1) and lambda is real with lambda >= 1 (PDF page 24; printed page 35, final sentence of Remark 2.7.9).
hypotheses: The local Taylor discussion assumes E X = 0 and Var(X) = 1 (PDF page 23; printed page 34, sentence beginning 'this kind of local bound').
For the displayed Taylor argument the source additionally says to assume, for simplicity, that X is bounded (PDF page 23; printed page 34, sentence beginning 'To see this').

The MGF conditions cross-referenced as the class characterizations carry the centering hypothesis E X = 0 (PDF page 13; printed page 24, 'Moreover, if E X = 0' before Proposition 2.5.2(v); PDF page 21; printed page 32, 'Moreover, if E X = 0' before Proposition 2.7.1(e)).

The counterexample distribution is the rate-one exponential distribution, which the surrounding Example 2.7.8 places in the sub-exponential class (PDF page 23; printed page 34, Example 2.7.8; PDF page 24; printed page 35, final sentence of Remark 2.7.9).
conclusions: As lambda tends to 0, the MGF of the bounded centered unit-variance X has the displayed second-order approximation E exp(lambda X) approximately 1 + lambda^2/2 approximately exp(lambda^2/2), obtained by retaining 1, lambda X, and lambda^2 X^2/2 with a stated o(lambda^2 X^2) remainder inside the expectation (PDF page 23; printed page 34, displayed formula in Remark 2.7.9).

For X distributed as N(0,1), the comparison is exact: E exp(lambda X) = exp(lambda^2/2) for every real lambda (PDF page 13; printed page 24, equation (2.12); PDF page 24; printed page 35, first sentence).

For centered sub-gaussian distributions, a quadratic-exponential MGF upper bound of this form holds for every real lambda and characterizes the sub-gaussian class, with constants as in Proposition 2.5.2(v) (PDF page 24; printed page 35, sentences beginning 'For sub-gaussian distributions'; PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(v)).

For centered sub-exponential distributions, a quadratic-exponential MGF upper bound of this form is required only for sufficiently small lambda and characterizes the sub-exponential class, concretely for |lambda| <= 1/K_5 with the constants of Proposition 2.7.1(e) (PDF page 24; printed page 35, sentence beginning 'And for sub-exponential distributions'; PDF page 21; printed page 32, Proposition 2.7.1(e)).

No analogous general large-lambda MGF bound is available for all sub-exponential distributions: for X distributed as Exp(1), E exp(lambda X) is infinite whenever lambda >= 1 (PDF page 24; printed page 35, final sentence of Remark 2.7.9).
definitions_and_conventions: The MGF under discussion is the expectation E exp(lambda X), as used throughout Remark 2.7.9 and in the cross-referenced MGF properties (PDF pages 23-24; printed pages 34-35, Remark 2.7.9; PDF page 13, printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(v); PDF page 21, printed page 32, Proposition 2.7.1(e)).

The standard-normal normalization is mean zero and variance one, and its MGF formula is exp(lambda^2/2) (PDF page 13; printed page 24, equation (2.12); PDF page 23; printed page 34, phrase 'mean zero and unit variance').

In the sub-gaussian property the bound is E exp(lambda X) <= exp(K_5^2 lambda^2) for all real lambda; in the sub-exponential property the same functional bound is imposed only when |lambda| <= 1/K_5 (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(v); PDF page 21; printed page 32, Proposition 2.7.1(e)).
The source's Exp(1) notation means the exponential distribution of rate one, inherited from Example 2.7.8's definition of Exp(lambda) (PDF page 23; printed page 34, Example 2.7.8).
implicit_context: The phrases 'bound like this' and 'this bound' refer back to the quadratic-exponential MGF bounds in Proposition 2.5.2(v) and Proposition 2.7.1(e), not to literal equality with exp(lambda^2/2) for every member of either class (PDF page 24; printed page 35, comparison paragraph; PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(v); PDF page 21; printed page 32, Proposition 2.7.1(e)).

The centering assumption is inherited from the 'Moreover, if E X = 0' clauses that introduce both cross-referenced MGF characterizations (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2; PDF page 21; printed page 32, Proposition 2.7.1).

The local calculation uses E X = 0 to remove the linear term and unit variance to replace E X^2 by 1 in the displayed value 1 + lambda^2/2 (PDF page 23; printed page 34, hypothesis sentence and displayed Taylor approximation; this connection is the analyst's structural reading of adjacent source statements).

The rate-one exponential example concerns failure on the positive-lambda side at and beyond lambda = 1; the source does not state a symmetric negative-lambda failure (PDF page 24; printed page 35, final sentence of Remark 2.7.9).

semantic_facets.topic: local asymptotic rather than exact identity
details: For a general bounded centered unit-variance X, the displayed relation uses approximation symbols and is asserted only as lambda tends to 0 (PDF page 23; printed page 34, Remark 2.7.9 displayed formula).
Exact equality is separately asserted only for the standard normal example via equation (2.12) (PDF page 24; printed page 35, first sentence; PDF page 13; printed page 24, equation (2.12)).
The sub-gaussian characterization quantifies over every real lambda (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(v)).
The sub-exponential characterization quantifies only over |lambda| <= 1/K_5 (PDF page 21; printed page 32, Proposition 2.7.1(e)).
The exponential counterexample asserts divergence for lambda >= 1 (PDF page 24; printed page 35, final sentence).
The illustrative local expansion is for mean-zero, unit-variance X and additionally assumes boundedness for simplicity (PDF page 23; printed page 34, Remark 2.7.9).

Both cited distribution-class MGF characterizations are introduced under E X = 0, but their scale is encoded by K_5 rather than a unit-variance normalization (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(v); PDF page 21; printed page 32, Proposition 2.7.1(e)).
The remark says the all-lambda bound characterizes sub-gaussian distributions and the small-lambda bound characterizes sub-exponential distributions (PDF page 24; printed page 35, middle paragraph).
The Exp(1) example shows why the sub-exponential characterization cannot in general be extended to large positive lambda (PDF page 24; printed page 35, final sentence).

undebatable_constraints: Retain all three hypotheses in the local illustration: X is bounded (stated 'for simplicity'), E X = 0, and Var(X) = 1 (PDF page 23; printed page 34, Remark 2.7.9).

Represent the general-X Taylor conclusion as a near-zero approximation/asymptotic claim, not as exact equality or as an all-lambda inequality (PDF page 23; printed page 34, displayed approximation and 'as lambda -> 0').

Preserve the exact standard-normal identity E exp(lambda X) = exp(lambda^2/2) for all real lambda as a separate special case (PDF page 13; printed page 24, equation (2.12); PDF page 24; printed page 35).

Preserve the different lambda domains of the two characterization bounds: all real lambda for centered sub-gaussian variables and |lambda| <= 1/K_5 for centered sub-exponential variables (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(v); PDF page 21; printed page 32, Proposition 2.7.1(e)).
Do not omit the claim that these respective global and local MGF bounds characterize the sub-gaussian and sub-exponential classes (PDF page 24; printed page 35, comparison paragraph).
Do not omit or symmetrize the stated failure example: X distributed as Exp(1) has infinite MGF for lambda >= 1 (PDF page 24; printed page 35, final sentence).

Do not silently replace the class bounds exp(K_5^2 lambda^2) by the standard-normal identity exp(lambda^2/2); the cross-referenced propositions use distribution-dependent scale constants (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(v); PDF page 21; printed page 32, Proposition 2.7.1(e)).

ambiguities.impact: A formal restatement must choose a precise asymptotic formulation, such as a little-o expansion, and that choice should be identified as a sharpening of the source's informal display rather than quoted as literal source syntax.

ambiguities.issue: The Exp(1) counterexample is not centered, whereas the quadratic MGF characterizations in the cited propositions are stated under a centering hypothesis.
ambiguities.evidence: Example 2.7.8 on PDF page 23, printed page 34 gives the exponential distribution mean as 1/lambda; Remark 2.7.9 on PDF page 24, printed page 35 uses X distributed as Exp(1); Propositions 2.5.2(v) and 2.7.1(e) explicitly assume E X = 0.
ambiguities.impact: The source explicitly supports the stated uncentered counterexample to a general large-positive-lambda bound; any claim about the centered variable X - E X would be a further inference and is not silently inserted into the contract.

contract_plain_english: Remark 2.7.9 says that if X has mean zero and variance one, and is assumed bounded for simplicity, then near lambda = 0 its MGF has the same second-order behavior as the standard normal: E exp(lambda X) is approximately 1 + lambda^2/2 and hence approximately exp(lambda^2/2) (PDF page 23; printed page 34). For N(0,1) this is the exact identity E exp(lambda X) = exp(lambda^2/2) for every real lambda (PDF page 13; printed page 24, equation (2.12); PDF page 24; printed page 35). The corresponding centered sub-gaussian characterization gives a quadratic-exponential upper bound for all real lambda, whereas the centered sub-exponential characterization requires it only near zero, specifically for |lambda| <= 1/K_5 with the proposition's scale constant (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(v); PDF page 21; printed page 32, Proposition 2.7.1(e); PDF page 24; printed page 35). The local restriction is essential in general: the source's sub-exponential example X distributed as Exp(1) has infinite MGF for lambda >= 1 (PDF pages 23-24; printed pages 34-35, Example 2.7.8 and Remark 2.7.9).
